top_evidence.document_title: Endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection for colorectal laterally spreading tumors (> 20 mm): a systematic review and meta-analysis
top_evidence.text: The reporting of this systematic review follows the recommendations of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (Supplementary Material 1) [10]. Quality assessment: Search strategy: The risk of bias was assessed independently by two reviewers (Q.Z. and T.K.) using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB 2) for randomized trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for nonrandomized controlled studies. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or by consulting a third reviewer (T.Z.). An electronic literature search was conducted by an experienced librarian with supervision from the study's principal investigator. Multiple databases were searched from inception to 1 May 2025, to identify eligible studies. The databases searched included PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane. The search strategies employed in PubMed and Cochrane Library databases were as follows: (((colorectal tumors) OR (laterally spreading tumor)) AND (endoscopic submucosal dissection) OR (ESD)) AND ((piecemeal endoscopic mucosal resection) OR (pEMR) OR (piecemeal EMR) OR (pmEMR) OR (EMR-precutting) OR (EMR-P) OR (endoscopic piecemeal mucosal resection) OR(EPMR)). The search strategy applied in the Embase database was: (colorectal AND ('tumors'/exp OR tumors) OR laterally) AND spreading AND ('tumor'/exp OR tumor) AND (endoscopic AND submucosal AND ('dissection'/exp OR dissection) OR esd) AND (((piecemeal AND endoscopic AND mucosal AND ('resection'/exp OR resection) OR pemr OR piecemeal) AND emr OR pmemr OR 'emr precutting' OR 'emr p' OR endoscopic) AND piecemeal AND mucosal AND ('resection'/exp OR resection) OR epmr).

top_evidence.text: Most studies included in this meta-analysis were single-center or retrospective in nature. To minimize the risk of bias, we used the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale to assess the quality of nonrandomized studies. Furthermore, owing to missing original data, we were unable to compare the potential impact of different LST subtypes or lesion locations (e.g., proximal colon versus distal colon/rectum) on the efficacy and safety of the two techniques. Since different subtypes and locations may vary in biological behavior, technical difficulty, and prognosis (e.g., more advanced histology such as high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia or intramucosal carcinoma may increase the difficulty of en bloc resection), the absence of this information may affect the interpretation of the results. Future prospective, multicenter studies, especially those collecting detailed lesion characteristics, are needed to more comprehensively evaluate the value of ESD and EMR in different clinical scenarios. top_evidence.section: Results > Statistical Analysis > Search Results And Population Characteristics
top_evidence.text: Statistical analyses were performed using the Cochrane Collaboration's RevMan 5.4 software. Statistical analyses were performed using the Cochrane Collaboration's RevMan 5.4 software. Data were analyzed using randomeffects models, with forest plots generated for each outcome. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Heterogeneity was assessed via Q -test and I 2 statistics. Sensitivity analysis employed the leave-one-out method to evaluate robustness. Publication bias was initially evaluated through funnel plot visualization and confirmed with Egger's test (Stata 18.0). Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05 (heterogeneity threshold: p < 0.1). A total of 111 duplicate records were excluded using EndNote. After removing reviews, meta-analyses, letters, editorials, case reports/series, and ineligible publications, eight studies were ultimately included (see PRISMA flowchart, Fig. 1). The analysis comprised 3024 patients: 1451 underwent ESD and 1573 received EMR (including 588 piecemeal EMR procedures). Included studies consisted of one RCT and seven retrospective studies (six single-center, two multicenter), with geographical distribution as follows: three from South Korea, three from Japan, one from Germany, and one from France. Detailed study characteristics are summarized in Table 1. We used the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for nonrandomized studies to assess methodology quality, which gave a mean score of 7.7 (range 6-9) (Table 2) [18]. For the randomized trials, we used Cochrane's Risk of Bias assessment (Table 3) [19]. General characteristics of the studies and characteristics of the included lesions were shown in Table 1.

top_evidence.text: The GRADE working group approach was used to rate the quality of evidence. Based on the predominance of observational studies and negligible heterogeneity ( I 2 < 5%), the overall evidence was rated as low certainty. However, for local recurrence, the certainty was upgraded to moderate due to the very large magnitude of effect (OR 0.06).

top_evidence.document_title: Endoscopic submucosal dissection versus endoscopic mucosal resection for colorectal laterally spreading tumors (> 20 mm): a systematic review and meta-analysis
top_evidence.text: Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), as a minimally invasive technique, has been widely recognized as an effective approach for the management of superficial colorectal tumors larger than 2 cm. Compared with conventional surgery, ESD offers significant advantages in terms of patient tolerability, faster recovery, and greater cost-effectiveness Table 1 Main characteristics of the included studies Table 2 Risk of bias across studies assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale [20]. One of the key findings of this meta-analysis is the significant superiority of ESD in reducing recurrence rates of colorectal laterally spreading tumors (LSTs) larger than 20 mm. The overall recurrence rates in the ESD and EMR groups were 0.62% and 12.02%, respectively, which aligns closely with the results of studies such as that by Russo et al. [21]. The higher recurrence rate in the EMR group observed in this meta-analysis is associated with both lesion size and the use of piecemeal resection [14, 22, 23]. This is further supported by the findings of Motomi Terasaki et al., who reported that the local recurrence rate for 40 mm LSTs was significantly higher than that for 20-39 mm lesions ( p < 0.001), and that lesions resected in three or more pieces had a notably higher recurrence rate compared with those resected in two pieces or en bloc ( p = 0.013). Similarly, in the study by Yutaka Saito et al., the recurrence rate was approximately 2% in the ESD group compared with approximately 14% in the EMR group, and recurrence after EMR occurred more frequently in piecemeal resection cases. Therefore, when lesions are large and piecemeal resection is anticipated (especially > 40 mm), ESD may be preferred to reduce the risk of recurrence. In contrast, if EMR can achieve en bloc or limited-piece resection, the recurrence risk appears to be relatively controllable. These results highlight the crucial role of resection completeness and lesion size in recurrence risk. piecemeal resection significantly increases the risk of incomplete removal, renders precise histological margin assessment (R0 resection) extremely challenging, and makes it difficult to ensure complete eradication of neoplastic tissue. Residual adenomatous tissue has been shown to have a rapid regenerative capacity and may increase the risk of recurrence [24, 25]. The high proportion of piecemeal resections in the EMR group directly explains its significantly elevated recurrence rate. In addition to the technical comparison between ESD and EMR, the use of adjuvant thermal ablation techniques-such as snare tip soft coagulation (STSC) or argon plasma coagulation (APC)-applied to the resection margins following piecemeal EMR has emerged as a promising strategy to reduce local recurrence. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Chandan et al. demonstrated that STSC after EMR for LSTs > 20 mm significantly lowered adenoma recurrence at the first surveillance colonoscopy (pooled rate: 6%; OR 0.27, p < 0.001) [26]. Similarly, a recent meta-analysis of randomized trials by Santo et al. confirmed that thermal ablation (including both STSC and APC) of post-EMR margins reduced recurrence rates (RR = 0.31, p < 0.001) without increasing the risk of adverse events or delayed bleeding [27]. These findings suggest that margin ablation may serve as a safe and effective adjunct to EMR, particularly in settings where ESD is not readily available or feasible. However, its implementation should be guided by lesion characteristics and endoscopist expertise, and future studies should directly compare EMR with adjuvant ablation versus ESD in large LSTs. Because all lesions analyzed in this study were larger than 20 mm, en bloc resection is often difficult to achieve using conventional EMR, necessitating widespread adoption of piecemeal resection. This approach has inherent drawbacks: Table 3 Cochrane Collaboration tool to assess risk of bias Owing to the difficulty in assessing margins after piecemeal resection, this study omitted the evaluation of R0 resection rate, which further underscores the pathological assessment differences between the two techniques and their implications for follow-up management. Based on the current study and literature evidence [13, 23, 28], we recommend that patients who achieve curative en bloc ESD, given their extremely low recurrence risk, should undergo standard surveillance colonoscopy at 1 year postprocedure. In contrast, for cases managed with piecemeal ESD or any EMR, due to the significantly increased risk of residual lesion and recurrence, we strongly recommend shortening the surveillance interval to 6 months to enable early detection and intervention for residual or recurrent lesions. In terms of safety, the risk of perforation with ESD is higher, a concern that is particularly prominent in Western countries, leading to EMR being more commonly adopted as the mainstream approach [29]. Our findings are consistent with this, showing a higher perforation risk for ESD compared with EMR. Right-sided colonic lesions and longer procedure duration are significant risk factors for ESD-related perforation, while lesion size itself is not directly associated with perforation risk [30, 31]. This suggests that, in the hands of experienced endoscopists, even larger lesions can be safely managed without a proportional increase in perforation risk, which carries important clinical implications. Endoscopists should exercise particular caution during ESD for right-sided LSTs. Technological advancements are crucial for reducing perforation risk; for example, Okamoto et al. demonstrated that the use of novel Mucosectomy knives during ESD significantly shortened procedure time and reduced the risk of perforation [32]. Notably, the widespread adoption of ESD is limited by its steep learning curve. The number of procedures required to achieve proficiency varies considerably based on training pathways. In structured, tutored settings such as those in Japan, trainees may achieve competence after approximately 30-40 colorectal ESDs [33, 34]. However, in Western countries, where an untutored, prevalence-based approach is often adopted, the learning curve is substantially longer, with some studies reporting a requirement of up to 280 procedures to achieve expertlevel resection speed and safety [35]. These differences underscore the importance of dedicated training programs, mentorship, and case selection during the initial learning phase to optimize outcomes and minimize complications. This underscores the importance of systematic training and accumulation of surgical experience. Our study also showed that the vast majority of perforations could be managed successfully with endoscopic clipping or conservative treatment, with only a minority requiring surgical intervention, indicating that ESD is controllable and safe in experienced hands. Fig. 2 Forest plot, local recurrence rate Fig. 3 Evaluation of publication bias for recurrence using funnel plot No significant difference was observed between ESD and EMR in terms of postprocedural bleeding, with overall bleeding rates of 3.65% and 3.75%, respectively. Rectal location and longer ESD procedure time have been identified as risk factors for post-ESD bleeding [30]. Of note, Motomi Terasaki et al. found that in comparison with conventional ESD, hybrid ESD (lesions were resected by snaring after circumferential incision and limited submucosal dissection), which significantly shortens operative time, was associated with no delayed bleeding events. This suggests that optimizing procedural workflow and reducing operative time may help decrease bleeding complications. The vast majority of bleeding episodes were successfully managed with endoscopic clipping without the need for transfusion or additional surgery.
